summary.text: Separating the factors divisible by $p$ expresses each successive binomial ratio as $\prod_{p\nmid j}(1+\beta p^r/j)$; expanding this product and pairing $j$ with $p^r-j$ gives strong $p$-adic bounds for the reciprocal harmonic sums, isolating the quadratic main term $-\beta(\beta+1)p^{2r}H_2/2$ with a sufficiently divisible remainder. For $p\ge5$, $\binom{\alpha p^s}{p^s}\equiv\alpha\pmod{p^3}$ forces an extra $p^3$ in the leading coefficient, while for $p=3$ the congruences modulo $27$ and $9$ together with sharper cubic-sum and remainder bounds supply the missing valuation.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
a(n)=\binom{3n}{n}^{2}-27\binom{2n}{n}.
\]
We prove that, for every prime \(p\ge 3\) and every \(r\ge2\),
\[
a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.
\]
Throughout, \(v_p\) denotes the usual \(p\)-adic valuation on nonzero rational numbers; an assertion \(v_p(x)\ge m\) is understood to be automatically true when \(x=0\). We repeatedly use
\[
v_p(xy)=v_p(x)+v_p(y),\qquad
v_p(x+y)\ge \min\{v_p(x),v_p(y)\}.
\]
All rational numbers occurring below have denominators prime to \(p\), except for the explicitly displayed powers of \(p\), so these valuation estimates can ultimately be translated directly into integer divisibility.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Splitting the binomial product into its \(p\)-divisible and \(p\)-free parts
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For \(s\ge1\), put
\[
U_s=\{j:1\le j\le p^s,\ p\nmid j\}
\]
and define the inverse-power sums
\[
H_t^{(s)}=\sum_{j\in U_s}\frac1{j^t}\qquad(t\ge1).
\]
For an integer \(\alpha\ge1\), define
\[
P_\alpha^{(s)}=
\prod_{j\in U_s}\left(1+\frac{(\alpha-1)p^s}{j}\right).
\]

The elementary product formula
\[
\binom{\alpha n}{n}
 =\prod_{i=1}^{n}\frac{(\alpha-1)n+i}{i}
\]
applied with \(n=p^s\) can be split according as \(p\mid i\) or \(p\nmid i\). If \(i=pt\), then
\[
\frac{(\alpha-1)p^s+pt}{pt}
 =\frac{(\alpha-1)p^{s-1}+t}{t}.
\]
The product over all multiples of \(p\) therefore equals
\(\binom{\alpha p^{s-1}}{p^{s-1}}\), while the product over the remaining indices is \(P_\alpha^{(s)}\). Hence
\[
\boxed{
\binom{\alpha p^s}{p^s}
 =\binom{\alpha p^{s-1}}{p^{s-1}}P_\alpha^{(s)}.}
\tag{1}
\]

We next obtain sufficiently precise approximations to \(P_\alpha^{(s)}\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Valuation estimates for the harmonic sums
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We first record a lifting argument. Every member of \(U_s\), for \(s\ge2\), has a unique expression
\[
j=b+a p^{s-1},\qquad b\in U_{s-1},\quad 0\le a<p.
\tag{2}
\]
Indeed, take \(b\) to be the remainder modulo \(p^{s-1}\); because \(p\nmid j\), this remainder is nonzero and not divisible by \(p\).

Fix \(b\in U_{s-1}\), and set
\[
x_a=\frac{a p^{s-1}}b.
\]
Then
\[
(b+a p^{s-1})^{-t}=b^{-t}(1+x_a)^{-t}.
\]
Since \(v_p(x_a)\ge s-1\), the expansion of \((1+x)^{-t}\) gives
\[
(1+x_a)^{-t}=1-tx_a+R_a,
\qquad v_p(R_a)\ge2(s-1).
\tag{3}
\]
Also
\[
\sum_{a=0}^{p-1}x_a
 =\frac{p^{s-1}}b\frac{p(p-1)}2,
\]
which has valuation at least \(s\), because \(p\ge3\). As \(s\ge2\), the sum of the remainders in (3) also has valuation at least \(s\). Summing over \(a\), we therefore obtain
\[
\sum_{a=0}^{p-1}(b+a p^{s-1})^{-t}
 =b^{-t}(p+\delta_b),
\qquad v_p(\delta_b)\ge s.
\]
Summing over \(b\in U_{s-1}\) gives
\[
\boxed{H_t^{(s)}=pH_t^{(s-1)}+\Delta_s,
\qquad v_p(\Delta_s)\ge s.}
\tag{4}
\]

At level one, the nonzero residue classes modulo \(p\) form a cyclic multiplicative group of order \(p-1\). Consequently,
\[
\sum_{j=1}^{p-1}j^m\equiv0\pmod p
\quad\text{if }p-1\nmid m.
\tag{5}
\]
Since \(j^{-t}\equiv j^{t(p-2)}\pmod p\), and multiplication by \(p-2\) is invertible modulo \(p-1\), (5) implies
\[
v_p(H_t^{(1)})\ge1
\quad\text{if }p-1\nmid t.
\tag{6}
\]
This argument with rational sums is legitimate after multiplying by \(((p-1)!)^t\), which is a \(p\)-adic unit.

Induction using (4) now yields two basic estimates:
\[
\boxed{v_p(H_t^{(s)})\ge s-1\quad\text{for every }t,}
\tag{7}
\]
and, whenever \(p-1\nmid t\),
\[
\boxed{v_p(H_t^{(s)})\ge s.}
\tag{8}
\]
In particular, for every \(p\ge3\), (8) applies to \(t=1\). For \(p\ge5\), it also applies to \(t=2\).

We need sharper estimates obtained by pairing \(j\) with \(N-j\), where \(N=p^s\). This pairing permutes \(U_s\), and its denominators are all \(p\)-adic units. Direct algebra gives
\[
H_1^{(s)}+\frac N2H_2^{(s)}
 =\frac{N^2}{2}
 \sum_{j\in U_s}\frac1{j^2(N-j)}.
\tag{9}
\]
The sum on the right is \(p\)-integral, so initially (9) gives valuation at least \(2s\).

A second set of pairing identities provides stronger information. Define
\[
S=\sum_{j\in U_s}\frac1{j^2(N-j)^2},\qquad
T=\sum_{j\in U_s}\frac1{j^3(N-j)^3}.
\]
First,
\[
\frac1{j^2(N-j)^2}-\frac1{j^4}
 =\frac{N(2j-N)}{j^4(N-j)^2}.
\]
Every denominator here is a \(p\)-adic unit, and the right side has valuation at least \(s\). Together with (7) for \(H_4^{(s)}\), this yields
\[
\boxed{v_p(S)\ge s-1.}
\tag{10}
\]
Next, adding the reciprocal cubes at paired arguments gives
\[
\boxed{
2H_3^{(s)}
 =N\bigl(-3S+N^2T\bigr).}
\tag{11}
\]
The sum \(T\) is \(p\)-integral. Thus (10) and (11) imply, for all \(p\ge3\),
\[
\boxed{v_p(H_3^{(s)})\ge2s-1.}
\tag{12}
\]
When \(p=3\), the coefficient \(3\) in \(-3S\) supplies one more factor of \(3\); hence
\[
\boxed{v_3(H_3^{(s)})\ge2s.}
\tag{13}
\]

To sharpen (9), direct partial-fraction algebra gives
\[
\sum_{j\in U_s}\frac1{j^2(N-j)}
 =-H_3^{(s)}-NH_4^{(s)}
 +N^2\sum_{j\in U_s}\frac1{j^4(N-j)}.
\tag{14}
\]
The last sum is \(p\)-integral. By (7), (12), and (14), the sum on the left has valuation at least \(2s-1\). Substitution into (9) therefore gives the important cancellation
\[
\boxed{
v_p\left(H_1^{(s)}+\frac{p^s}{2}H_2^{(s)}\right)
 \ge4s-1.}
\tag{15}
\]
Writing \(H_1^{(s)}\) as this quantity minus \(p^sH_2^{(s)}/2\), and using (7), also gives
\[
\boxed{v_p(H_1^{(s)})\ge2s-1.}
\tag{16}
\]
For \(p\ge5\), (8) for \(t=2\) and the weaker valuation \(2s\) already available from (9) give the familiar stronger form
\[
\boxed{v_p(H_1^{(s)})\ge2s\qquad(p\ge5).}
\tag{17}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Expansion of the \(p\)-free product
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(e_m^{(s)}\) be the \(m\)-th elementary symmetric function of the numbers \(1/j\), \(j\in U_s\):
\[
e_m^{(s)}=
\sum_{\substack{A\subseteq U_s\\|A|=m}}
\prod_{j\in A}\frac1j.
\]
Thus \(e_0=1\), \(e_1=H_1\), and expansion of the product gives, with \(\beta=\alpha-1\),
\[
P_\alpha^{(s)}
 =\sum_{m\ge0}(\beta p^s)^m e_m^{(s)}.
\tag{18}
\]
All \(e_m^{(s)}\) are \(p\)-integral.

Newton’s identities give
\[
2e_2=H_1^2-H_2,
\tag{19}
\]
\[
3e_3=e_2H_1-H_1H_2+H_3,
\tag{20}
\]
and
\[
4e_4=e_3H_1-e_2H_2+H_1H_3-H_4.
\tag{21}
\]
Using (7), (12), and (16) in these identities yields
\[
v_p(e_2)\ge s-1,
\tag{22}
\]
\[
v_p(e_3)\ge2s-1-v_p(3),
\tag{23}
\]
and
\[
v_p(e_4)\ge s-1.
\tag{24}
\]
For \(p=3\), the strengthened estimate (13) used in (20) gives, for \(s\ge2\),
\[
\boxed{v_3(e_3)\ge2s-1.}
\tag{25}
\]
For \(p\ge5\), (8), (17), and (19) improve (22) to
\[
\boxed{v_p(e_2)\ge s.}
\tag{26}
\]

We now isolate the principal part of (18). Put
\[
\theta_s=H_1^{(s)}+\frac{p^s}{2}H_2^{(s)}.
\]
Combining the linear and quadratic terms in (18), using (19) and
\(H_1=\theta_s-p^sH_2/2\), gives the exact identity
\[
P_\alpha^{(s)}
 =1+M_\beta^{(s)}+E_\beta^{(s)},
\tag{27}
\]
where
\[
M_\beta^{(s)}
 =-\frac{\beta(\beta+1)}2p^{2s}H_2^{(s)}
\tag{28}
\]
and
\[
E_\beta^{(s)}
 =\beta p^s\theta_s
 +\frac{\beta^2}{2}p^{2s}(H_1^{(s)})^2
 +\sum_{m\ge3}(\beta p^s)^m e_m^{(s)}.
\tag{29}
\]

Let us estimate the error. By (15), the first term of (29) has valuation at least \(5s-1\). By (16), its second term has valuation at least
\(2s+2(2s-1)=6s-2\). In the remaining sum, the \(m=3\) term has valuation at least
\[
3s+(2s-1-v_p(3))=5s-1-v_p(3),
\]
the \(m=4\) term has valuation at least \(4s+s-1=5s-1\), and every term with \(m\ge5\) has valuation at least \(5s\), since \(e_m\) is \(p\)-integral. Therefore
\[
\boxed{v_p(E_\beta^{(s)})\ge5s-1-v_p(3).}
\tag{30}
\]
For \(p=3\) and \(s\ge2\), (25) removes the loss in the cubic term, so
\[
\boxed{v_3(E_\beta^{(s)})\ge5s-1.}
\tag{31}
\]

The principal term (28), together with (7), gives
\[
v_p(M_\beta^{(s)})\ge3s-1.
\]
Thus, for \(s\ge2\),
\[
\boxed{v_p(P_\alpha^{(s)}-1)\ge3s-1.}
\tag{32}
\]
For \(p\ge5\), (8) for \(H_2\) improves the principal term to valuation at least \(3s\), and (30) is much larger; hence
\[
\boxed{v_p(P_\alpha^{(s)}-1)\ge3s\qquad(p\ge5,\,s\ge2).}
\tag{33}
\]
The same product expansion, with the level-one estimates (6), also shows that for every \(s\ge1\),
\[
v_p(P_\alpha^{(s)}-1)\ge3\qquad(p\ge5).
\tag{34}
\]
For \(p=3\), the corresponding level-wise bound needed below is
\[
v_3(P_\alpha^{(s)}-1)\ge2\qquad(s\ge1).
\tag{35}
\]
For \(s\ge2\) this follows from (32), and at \(s=1\) it follows directly from (18), (6) for \(H_1\), (19), and the fact that every term of degree at least two already contains \(3^2\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Auxiliary binomial congruences and the leading coefficient
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Equation (1), together with (34), proves by induction on \(s\) that, for \(p\ge5\),
\[
\boxed{\binom{\alpha p^s}{p^s}\equiv\alpha\pmod {p^3}.}
\tag{36}
\]
Indeed, the assertion is clear for \(s=0\), and multiplication by
\(P_\alpha^{(s)}\equiv1\pmod {p^3}\) preserves it.

For \(p=3\), (35) similarly gives
\[
\boxed{\binom{2\cdot3^s}{3^s}\equiv2\pmod9.}
\tag{37}
\]
For \(\alpha=3\), one gains another factor because the preceding binomial coefficient is divisible by \(3\). Inductively,
\[
\boxed{\binom{3\cdot3^s}{3^s}\equiv3\pmod{27}.}
\tag{38}
\]
The base case is \(\binom31=3\). If the result holds at level \(s-1\), that binomial coefficient is divisible by \(3\); multiplying it by a factor congruent to \(1\pmod9\), as in (35), changes it by a multiple of \(27\). This proves (38).

We apply these congruences at level \(r-1\). Set
\[
C_3=\binom{3p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}},
\qquad
C_2=\binom{2p^{r-1}}{p^{r-1}},
\]
and define
\[
L=6C_3^2-27C_2.
\]
For \(p\ge5\), (36) gives \(C_3\equiv3\pmod{p^3}\) and
\(C_2\equiv2\pmod{p^3}\). Since
\[
L=6(C_3-3)(C_3+3)-27(C_2-2),
\tag{39}
\]
and \(6,27\) are \(p\)-adic units, we get
\[
\boxed{v_p(L)\ge3\qquad(p\ge5).}
\tag{40}
\]

For \(p=3\), (37) and (38) give
\[
v_3(C_3-3)\ge3,
\qquad v_3(C_2-2)\ge2.
\]
Moreover, \(C_3+3=(C_3-3)+6\), so \(v_3(C_3+3)\ge1\). In (39), the first term consequently has valuation at least
\(1+3+1=5\), while the second has valuation at least \(3+2=5\). Thus
\[
\boxed{v_3(L)\ge5.}
\tag{41}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Expansion of the difference and completion of the proof
--------------------------------------------------------------------

For brevity write
\[
P_3=P_3^{(r)},\quad P_2=P_2^{(r)},\quad
E_2=E_2^{(r)},\quad E_1=E_1^{(r)}.
\]
By (1),
\[
\binom{3p^r}{p^r}=C_3P_3,
\qquad
\binom{2p^r}{p^r}=C_2P_2.
\]
Hence
\[
a(p^r)-a(p^{r-1})
 =C_3^2(P_3^2-1)-27C_2(P_2-1).
\tag{42}
\]
From (27) and (28), for \(\beta=2\) and \(\beta=1\), respectively,
\[
P_3-1=-3p^{2r}H_2^{(r)}+E_2,
\qquad
P_2-1=-p^{2r}H_2^{(r)}+E_1.
\tag{43}
\]
Also
\[
P_3^2-1=2(P_3-1)+(P_3-1)^2.
\]
Substitution in (42), followed by collecting the principal terms, gives the exact identity
\[
\boxed{
\begin{aligned}
a(p^r)-a(p^{r-1})={}&
-p^{2r}H_2^{(r)}(6C_3^2-27C_2)\\
&+2C_3^2E_2-27C_2E_1
 +C_3^2(P_3-1)^2.
\end{aligned}}
\tag{44}
\]
We estimate the four terms separately. The binomial coefficients are integers, so they have nonnegative \(p\)-adic valuation.

First suppose \(p\ge5\). By (8),
\[
v_p(p^{2r}H_2^{(r)})\ge3r.
\]
Together with (40), the first term in (44) has valuation at least
\(3r+3\). By (30), now with \(v_p(3)=0\), each \(E_i\) has valuation at least \(5r-1\). Since \(r\ge2\),
\[
5r-1\ge3r+3.
\]
Thus the second and third terms also have valuation at least \(3r+3\). Finally, by (33),
\[
v_p((P_3-1)^2)\ge6r\ge3r+3.
\]
All four terms in (44), and hence their sum, have valuation at least \(3r+3\).

Now suppose \(p=3\). By (7),
\[
v_3(3^{2r}H_2^{(r)})\ge2r+(r-1)=3r-1.
\]
Together with (41), the first term of (44) has valuation at least
\(3r+4\), in particular at least \(3r+3\). By the exceptional estimate (31),
\[
v_3(E_i)\ge5r-1.
\]
The coefficient \(2C_3^2\) has nonnegative valuation, and the coefficient \(27C_2\) has valuation at least \(3\), so the second and third terms have valuation at least \(3r+3\) because \(5r-1\ge3r+3\) for \(r\ge2\). Finally, (32) gives
\[
v_3((P_3-1)^2)\ge2(3r-1)=6r-2\ge3r+3
\]
for \(r\ge2\). Thus every term of (44) again has valuation at least \(3r+3\).

We have proved in all cases that
\[
v_p\bigl(a(p^r)-a(p^{r-1})\bigr)\ge3r+3.
\]
The expression in parentheses is an integer. Therefore it is divisible by
\(p^{3r+3}\), which is precisely
\[
\boxed{a(p^r)\equiv a(p^{r-1})\pmod {p^{3r+3}}.}
\]
This completes the proof.
